newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary farm protests move into the capital.
newsitem.headline: Hungary farm protests move into the capital.

text.p: Hungary's agricultural protests reached the streets of Budapest for the first time on Tuesday as farmers from outside the capital brought tractors to Parliament to present demands for government support.
Around 130 tractors drove into the centre of the city, slowing down but not stopping traffic.
"We can't make a living," said 35-year-old Jozsef Vegh, from the village of Alsonemedi. "Hungary's agriculture needs a complete overhaul with all parties and the farmers involved in the talks."

The farmers represented a splinter group from the main group of protesters, based in Kiskoros in central Hungary, who have organised blockades throughout Hungary for the last three weeks against changes in tax laws and social security payments.

"The Kiskoros farmers have got bogged down in detail on taxes and social security," said Ferenc Takacs, 23. "We'll gladly pay tax if we can generate something to pay tax on and if all those rich people who turn farms into hunting lodges for tourists also pay their taxes."
"They're importing Dutch potatoes and we can't sell ours," shouted one farmer as he distributed free potatoes to passers-by.
The rest of Hungary saw fewer road blocks than on Monday but police said protesters were present at more than 100 locations.
The farmers blocked only one lane at a time, slowing traffic but allowing vehicles to pass, police said, adding that there were no reports of any violence.
The government has hardened its stance on negotiating with the farmers since the Kiskoros farmers' group snubbed Prime Minister Gyula Horn last week by failing to turn up at a meeting.

Agriculture Minister Frigyes Nagy, in unveiling a long-awaited draft of a new medium-term farming policy last Friday, said Hungarian agriculture had managed a trade surplus of $2 billion last year "despite its present crisis".
Hungary's Socialist Party promised a comprehensive overhaul of the country's ailing agriculture before coming to power in the summer of 1994.
